pool.prompt: The design stencil on a pole butt says '40 ft.' Your field measurement from ground line to pole top is 45 ft. What is the correct field action?
choices: Use the stenciled 40 ft because the factory stencil is always correct
Use your field measurement of 45 ft and discard the stencil as inaccurate
Record both the stenciled value (40 ft) and your field measurement (45 ft), note the 5 ft discrepancy, and flag for design engineer review
Re-measure from the road surface instead of the ground line to reconcile the two values
pool.explanation: Both values are data points, not one-right-one-wrong. The stencil reflects manufactured length; the field measurement reflects actual above-grade height, which depends on burial depth. Record both, note the discrepancy, and flag — the design engineer decides which value to use.

pool.prompt: During a pole audit, the gap between the highest existing telecom attachment (22 ft) and the proposed fiber height (23 ft) is 1 ft. What is the correct field action?
choices: Approve the attachment — 1 ft gap is fine for telecom standards
Reject the attachment — 1 ft gap is below the minimum and the pole must be replaced
Record the 1 ft gap, add a make-ready flag to the audit record, and pass the data to the design engineer for formal clearance analysis
Move the proposed fiber to 25 ft to create more clearance and update the design drawing
pool.explanation: A 1 ft gap warrants a make-ready flag, but the field walker does not make the final determination — the design engineer applies formal clearance requirements. Field triage says 'flag it'; the field walker never approves/rejects an attachment or modifies the proposed design.

pool.prompt: What term describes all current utility attachments on a pole — by carrier name, attachment type, and measured height?
choices: Load census
Existing occupancy
Attachment audit summary
Pole tag registry
pool.explanation: Existing occupancy is the baseline inventory the design engineer uses to determine whether a new attachment can be added without make-ready work. Accurate existing-occupancy documentation also protects the project sponsor during OTMR coordination.

pool.prompt: A field crew sees a pole with only 6 inches of clearance below the power company's neutral wire and decides to skip formal audit documentation since the make-ready need is 'obvious.' What's wrong with this approach?
choices: Nothing — experienced crews can skip documentation when the outcome is obvious
The crew should have climbed the pole to confirm the measurement before deciding
Without documented attachment heights and a formal audit record, the design engineer has no data to order make-ready or price the OTMR scope, and the flag is un-traceable if disputed later
The crew should have called the power company first before auditing joint-use poles
pool.explanation: Even when make-ready is visually obvious, skipping documentation creates downstream problems: the engineer can't run formal analysis without measured heights, the OTMR contractor can't scope work without a recorded inventory, and a disputed make-ready has no audit trail to reference.

pool.prompt: A crew misidentifies a pole's class during the audit — recording Class 4 (lighter) when it is actually Class 3 (stronger, heavier duty). What downstream consequence follows if this error goes uncaught until the RUS review stage?
choices: No consequence — pole class has no bearing on cost estimates or unit codes

The construction unit breakdown will show the wrong unit code, producing an incorrect materials list and cost estimate; if caught during RUS review, it triggers a deficiency finding and can add significant time to the review timeline
The contractor automatically corrects it without any documentation impact
RUS only verifies total pole count, never individual pole class
pool.explanation: Construction unit codes are specific to pole class and height — different classes are different unit codes with different material costs. An error propagates into the cost estimate and, if caught during RUS review, generates a deficiency finding requiring correction and resubmission.

pool.prompt: Why does the pole audit record both the stenciled pole length AND the field-measured height, rather than just recording whichever value seems more reliable?
choices: Recording both is unnecessary busywork with no engineering value

The discrepancy itself is meaningful information — it may indicate the pole was reset at a different depth than originally installed, which the design engineer needs to know when assessing structural capacity, not just the final height number
Only the stenciled value has any legal standing; the field measurement is purely optional
Recording both values is required only for RUS-funded projects, never for private projects
pool.explanation: A discrepancy between stenciled length and field-measured height can indicate a pole reset at a different burial depth than original installation — information relevant to structural assessment that recording only one value would obscure.

pool.prompt: What is the functional difference between a field crew's make-ready 'flag' and a make-ready 'approval' or 'rejection'?
choices: There is no difference; flag, approval, and rejection are interchangeable terms

A flag is a communication tool that alerts the design engineer to look closely at a specific pole during formal analysis; approval/rejection is a determination that only the design engineer (applying formal clearance rules) is authorized to make
Only the pole owner can flag a pole; field crews can only approve or reject
A flag automatically triggers pole replacement, while approval/rejection does not
pool.explanation: The field crew's role is limited to flagging conditions worth closer engineering review — not making the formal determination itself. This division of responsibility keeps engineering judgment calls with the design engineer, who applies the complete formal clearance analysis.

pool.prompt: Why is a pole audit considered a legal/engineering document rather than just a field convenience, even on jobs where make-ready needs seem visually self-evident?
choices: It has no legal significance; it exists purely for internal crew reference

The audit record supports formal engineering analysis, OTMR scope pricing, and dispute resolution with existing attachment carriers — without it, downstream decisions and any future disputes have no documented basis to reference
Legal significance only applies to audits performed by a licensed PE, never by field crews
The audit becomes a legal document only after construction is complete
pool.explanation: The audit record is the traceable basis for engineering determinations, OTMR contractor scoping, and — if an existing carrier disputes a make-ready requirement — the documentation that supports the project's position. Its legal/engineering weight exists from the moment it's created, not retroactively.
